questions.title: What Apex Is and When It's Actually Needed
questions.prompt: You've spent your career so far building everything with Flow. In plain terms, what is Apex, and what kind of requirement genuinely needs code instead of a declarative tool like Flow?
questions.modelAnswer: Apex is Salesforce's own strongly-typed, object-oriented programming language, syntactically close to Java, that compiles and runs directly on Salesforce's multitenant servers with SOQL and DML built right into the language. Flow should be the first instinct for most automation because it's visual, version-friendly, and maintainable by admins without a developer. Apex becomes genuinely necessary when a requirement needs something Flow can't express cleanly -- complex branching logic across unrelated collections of records, a callout that needs custom retry or error-handling behavior, logic that must ship with unit tests for a regulated process, or precise control over how a trigger processes a large bulk operation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by saying Apex isn't a replacement for Flow, it's the escape hatch for the handful of things Flow genuinely can't do well. I think of it like this: if I can draw the logic as a flowchart and it only touches a record or two in a predictable way, that's Flow. The moment I need real loops over unrelated data, a callout with retry logic, or something that has to be unit-tested because compliance cares, that's when I reach for Apex instead.
commonMistakes: Describing Apex as a scripting language instead of a compiled, strongly-typed one
Treating Apex as a wholesale replacement for Flow rather than a tool for specific gaps
Not knowing SOQL and DML are built directly into Apex's syntax
Reaching for Apex by default instead of evaluating whether Flow could handle it
Assuming Apex runs on a separate server rather than inside Salesforce's own execution context
keyPoints: Apex is a proprietary, Java-like, strongly-typed, compiled language
It runs server-side inside Salesforce's own multitenant execution context
SOQL and DML are native parts of the language, not external calls
Flow should be tried first; Apex is for genuine declarative gaps

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines what Apex is
Gives accurate, concrete reasons Apex is needed over Flow
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Lightning Web Components vs. Aura vs. Visualforce
questions.prompt: Salesforce has three different UI frameworks you might hear about -- Visualforce, Aura, and Lightning Web Components. What's each one, and which should a new project default to?
questions.modelAnswer: Visualforce is Salesforce's original, older markup-tag-based UI framework, tightly coupled to server-side controllers, from before Lightning Experience existed. Aura (the Lightning Component framework) was Salesforce's first attempt at a modern, component-based JavaScript framework running inside Lightning Experience. Lightning Web Components (LWC) is the newer standard, built on native, modern web standards -- Web Components, ES modules, and standard JavaScript classes -- rather than a proprietary framework, which makes it faster and lighter-weight than Aura. A new project should default to LWC; Salesforce itself recommends LWC for all new component development and Aura components can even host LWCs inside them if legacy interop is ever needed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lay it out as a timeline: Visualforce came first and still shows up in older orgs or very specific use cases like PDF generation, Aura came next as the first real component framework for Lightning, and LWC is what Salesforce has pushed as the standard since. For any new build today, I default to LWC without a second thought -- it's built on actual web standards instead of a proprietary framework, it renders faster, and it's what Salesforce is actively investing in. I'd only reach for Visualforce for something narrow like a PDF-rendering page, and I'd really only touch Aura if I'm maintaining something that already exists.
commonMistakes: Treating all three frameworks as equally current options for new work
Not knowing LWC is built on standard web technologies rather than a Salesforce-proprietary model
Assuming Visualforce is deprecated entirely rather than still useful for niche cases like PDFs
Confusing Aura components with LWC, since both run inside Lightning Experience
keyPoints: Visualforce is the oldest framework, server-controller-driven, pre-Lightning Experience
Aura was the first Lightning component framework, proprietary to Salesforce
LWC is built on native web standards (Web Components, ES modules) and is lighter and faster
LWC is Salesforce's recommended default for new component development

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes all three frameworks
Correctly recommends LWC as the default with sound reasoning
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Governor Limits -- Why They Exist
questions.prompt: What is a governor limit in Salesforce, and why does the platform enforce something like a 100-SOQL-query limit per transaction instead of just letting code run as long as it needs to?
questions.modelAnswer: A governor limit is a hard ceiling Salesforce enforces on resource usage within a single transaction -- things like the number of SOQL queries (100 in a synchronous transaction), DML statements, CPU time, and heap size -- and exceeding any one of them throws an unrecoverable runtime exception that rolls back the transaction. These limits exist because Salesforce is multitenant: thousands of unrelated customers share the exact same servers and database, so one org's poorly written, runaway code can't be allowed to consume unlimited resources and degrade performance for every other tenant on that same infrastructure. Governor limits are the mechanism that keeps one customer's bad code from becoming everyone's outage.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the apartment-building analogy: everyone shares the same building, the same water pressure, the same electrical grid, so the building has rules about how much any one unit can draw at once -- otherwise one tenant running every appliance at full blast knocks out power for the whole floor. Salesforce's governor limits are exactly that, applied to a shared multitenant platform. The 100-query limit specifically pushes you toward writing bulk-safe code -- querying once outside a loop instead of once per record inside it -- which is good practice anyway, but the limit is what actually forces the discipline instead of just recommending it.
commonMistakes: Describing governor limits as a bug or an arbitrary restriction rather than a deliberate design choice
Not connecting governor limits to the platform's multitenant architecture
Thinking limits can be raised simply by asking Salesforce support for more resources
Missing that hitting a governor limit throws an exception that rolls back the whole transaction
keyPoints: A governor limit is a hard per-transaction ceiling on resource usage (SOQL, DML, CPU, heap, and more)
Exceeding a governor limit throws an unrecoverable exception and rolls back the transaction
Limits exist because Salesforce's infrastructure is shared across many tenants
The limits force bulk-safe coding patterns rather than just recommending them

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a governor limit
Correctly ties the limits to multitenancy as the underlying reason
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Sandbox Types at a Glance
questions.prompt: Salesforce offers several sandbox types -- Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy, and Full. What actually differs between them, and which would you pick for a developer doing day-to-day Apex and LWC work?
questions.modelAnswer: The sandbox types differ mainly in storage capacity and whether they copy any production data. A Developer sandbox has a small storage allocation and copies no production data at all, just metadata -- it's meant for one developer's isolated work. Developer Pro is the same idea with more storage, suited for a small team or slightly larger customizations. Partial Copy sandboxes copy a configured sample of production data (via a sandbox template) along with metadata, useful for QA or testing against realistic-but-limited data. Full sandboxes are an exact copy of production, data and all, with production-level storage -- the most expensive and slowest to refresh, typically reserved for final staging/UAT or performance testing closest to production conditions. For day-to-day Apex and LWC development, a Developer sandbox is the right choice -- the developer doesn't need real data, just metadata and a safe place to write and unit-test code.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of the four sandbox types on two axes: how much data they bring with them, and how big they are. Developer sandboxes are the ones I live in day to day -- no real data, small storage, perfect for writing and testing code without worrying about touching anything sensitive. Developer Pro is just a bigger version of that for a team doing more substantial build work. Partial Copy is where I go when I actually need some realistic data to test against, like checking that a trigger behaves correctly against real-shaped records, without needing the entire production database. Full sandbox I reserve for the last stop before production -- UAT, performance testing, anything that genuinely needs production-scale data and storage -- because it's the slowest to refresh and the most resource-intensive.
commonMistakes: Assuming all sandbox types copy some amount of production data
Picking Full sandbox for routine development work it isn't needed for
Not knowing Partial Copy sandboxes rely on a sandbox template to define which data gets copied
Confusing sandbox refresh frequency limits with scratch org lifespan limits
keyPoints: Developer: no production data, small storage, for one developer
Developer Pro: no production data, larger storage, for small teams
Partial Copy: a sampled subset of production data via a template, for realistic testing
Full: exact copy of production data and storage, for final staging/UAT
Developer sandbox is the right everyday choice for Apex/LWC development

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes all four sandbox types
Correctly recommends Developer sandbox for the scenario with sound reasoning
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Scratch Orgs vs. Sandboxes
questions.prompt: What's a scratch org, and how is it fundamentally different from a sandbox? Why would a Salesforce DX-based development process prefer scratch orgs for day-to-day feature work?
questions.modelAnswer: A scratch org is a temporary, fully-configurable Salesforce org created on demand from a simple JSON definition file via the Salesforce CLI, source-tracked and disposable by design -- typically living days to a couple of weeks before being deleted and recreated fresh. A sandbox, by contrast, is a longer-lived copy derived from production, refreshed periodically rather than recreated from scratch, and its metadata state can drift silently from what's in version control over time. The Salesforce DX model prefers scratch orgs for day-to-day feature work because each scratch org is built entirely from source -- the exact metadata checked into Git -- guaranteeing the org matches what's in version control exactly, with no leftover configuration drift from a previous developer's changes; when the feature is done, the scratch org is simply thrown away.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd frame the difference: a sandbox is a place, a scratch org is a snapshot. A sandbox sits there, gets refreshed occasionally, and can quietly accumulate configuration nobody remembers adding. A scratch org gets built fresh, every time, straight from whatever's in my source-controlled project definition -- so if something's broken, I know it's broken in source, not because some stale manual change is still sitting in an environment from three sprints ago. That's exactly why source-driven development leans on scratch orgs for day-to-day feature work: it forces everything meaningful to live in version control, and the org itself becomes disposable and perfectly reproducible instead of a precious, hand-maintained thing I'm afraid to touch.
commonMistakes: Treating scratch orgs and sandboxes as interchangeable terms for the same concept
Not knowing scratch orgs are created from a JSON definition file via the Salesforce CLI
Missing that scratch orgs are meant to be disposable and recreated frequently
Not connecting scratch orgs to the source-driven development model behind Salesforce DX
keyPoints: A scratch org is created on demand from a JSON definition file via the Salesforce CLI
Scratch orgs are short-lived and disposable, typically recreated frequently
Sandboxes are longer-lived, production-derived, and refreshed rather than rebuilt from source
Scratch orgs guarantee the org matches source control, avoiding configuration drift

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines a scratch org and how it's created
Correctly contrasts it with a sandbox
Explains the source-driven development reasoning

questions.title: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Apex -- the Basic Shapes
questions.prompt: Salesforce gives you several ways to run Apex asynchronously -- Future methods, Queueable Apex, Batch Apex, and Scheduled Apex. At a beginner level, what's each one roughly for?
questions.modelAnswer: Future methods run a simple, fire-and-forget piece of logic on a separate thread later, often used for callouts from a context (like a trigger) that can't make callouts synchronously -- they're limited, can't easily chain, and don't accept sObjects as parameters. Queueable Apex is the more modern, flexible replacement for most future-method use cases -- it accepts complex parameter types including objects, can be chained (one queueable job enqueuing another), and returns a job ID for tracking. Batch Apex is built specifically for processing large numbers of records -- millions, if needed -- by breaking them into manageable chunks and running each chunk in its own governor-limit context, ideal for mass updates or cleanup jobs. Scheduled Apex simply runs a piece of logic (often a batch job) on a defined schedule, like a cron job, without anyone manually triggering it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe them by the job each one is actually built for. Future methods are the oldest, simplest async tool -- good for a quick callout you need off the main thread, but pretty limited otherwise. Queueable is what I reach for now instead of future methods almost every time, because it's just more capable -- it can take real objects as input and chain itself. Batch Apex is specifically for when I'm dealing with a genuinely large number of records and need the platform to chunk the work and give each chunk its own fresh governor limits. And Scheduled Apex is just the way I tell Salesforce 'run this batch job every night at 2am' without a person clicking a button.
commonMistakes: Treating all four async types as interchangeable options for any async need
Not knowing future methods can't accept sObjects as parameters
Confusing Batch Apex's chunking behavior with Queueable's single-execution model
Not recognizing Scheduled Apex is typically used to kick off a batch job rather than do heavy processing itself
keyPoints: Future methods: simple fire-and-forget, often for callouts, limited parameter types
Queueable Apex: more flexible, accepts objects, chainable, trackable via job ID
Batch Apex: processes large record volumes in chunks, each with fresh governor limits
Scheduled Apex: runs logic (often a batch job) on a defined recurring schedule

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes all four async Apex types
Gives an accurate use case for at least two of them
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: SOQL vs. SOSL
questions.prompt: What's the actual difference between SOQL and SOSL, and how would you decide which one to reach for when searching for a term that could be a first name, last name, or company name?
questions.modelAnswer: SOQL (Salesforce Object Query Language) queries one specific object (plus its related objects via relationship syntax) and is the right tool when you already know which object and which fields you're filtering on -- it's precise and structured, similar to SQL's SELECT statement. SOSL (Salesforce Object Search Language) performs a full-text search across multiple objects and multiple fields simultaneously, ranked by relevance, and is the right tool when you don't know in advance which object or field actually contains the match. For a search term that could be a first name, last name, or company name -- spanning Contact, Lead, and Account in ways you can't predict ahead of time -- SOSL is the better fit, since a single SOSL query can search across all of those objects and fields at once, where SOQL would require you to already commit to one specific object and field combination.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put it this way: SOQL is for when I already know the shape of what I'm looking for -- give me Contacts where LastName equals this, that's a SOQL question. SOSL is for when I genuinely don't know where the match is going to be -- someone typed a name into a global search box and it could be a Contact's first name, a Lead's company name, or an Account name, and I want one search that checks all of those at once. For that ambiguous name-or-company search, SOSL wins outright, because running three or four separate SOQL queries against different objects just to cover the same ground is both slower and messier than one SOSL call searching everything together.
commonMistakes: Treating SOQL and SOSL as interchangeable query tools
Not knowing SOSL can search across multiple objects in a single query while SOQL targets one object plus its relationships
Choosing SOQL for an ambiguous full-text search instead of SOSL
Not mentioning SOSL returns relevance-ranked results across object types
keyPoints: SOQL targets one object (plus related objects) with structured field filters
SOSL performs full-text search across multiple objects and fields at once
SOSL is the right choice when you don't know which object/field holds the match
SOQL is the right choice when the object and filter criteria are already known

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes SOQL from SOSL
Correctly answers the ambiguous-search scenario with SOSL
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What CRM Analytics Actually Is
questions.prompt: What is CRM Analytics (formerly Tableau CRM / Einstein Analytics), and what can it do that a standard Salesforce report or dashboard genuinely can't?
questions.modelAnswer: CRM Analytics is Salesforce's native business intelligence platform, built for exploring large datasets interactively, blending data from multiple sources (Salesforce and external systems), and surfacing AI-driven insights -- distinct from standard reports and dashboards, which are built directly against live Salesforce records in near-real time but with much more limited analytical depth. Standard reports are excellent for straightforward, record-level questions answerable within Salesforce's own report builder. CRM Analytics can do things standard reporting genuinely can't: it works against pre-aggregated, columnar datasets that support fast, interactive exploration of millions of rows, it can blend data from external sources (like a data warehouse) alongside Salesforce data in one view, and it supports predictive and AI-driven features that go beyond simple filtering and grouping.
questions.professionalAnswer: The simplest way I'd explain it to someone who's only ever built standard reports: a report is great when the question is simple and the data is already in Salesforce in a shape that's easy to filter and group. CRM Analytics is what I reach for when the question gets bigger than that -- when I need to blend Salesforce data with something from outside the platform, when the dataset is large enough that clicking through filters in a standard report gets painfully slow, or when I actually want the platform to surface a trend or prediction rather than me building every slice by hand. It's genuinely a different tool built for a different scale and kind of analysis, not just a fancier dashboard skin on top of the same reports.
commonMistakes: Describing CRM Analytics as just a prettier version of standard dashboards
Not knowing CRM Analytics can blend external, non-Salesforce data sources
Missing that CRM Analytics works against pre-aggregated datasets rather than live records
Not mentioning the AI/predictive capabilities as a genuine differentiator
keyPoints: CRM Analytics is Salesforce's native BI platform for deeper, large-scale analysis
It works against pre-aggregated, columnar datasets rather than live records
It can blend external data sources with Salesforce data in one view
It supports AI-driven and predictive insights beyond standard filtering/grouping

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what CRM Analytics is
Correctly identifies genuine capability gaps vs. standard reports

questions.title: Junction Objects for Many-to-Many Relationships
questions.prompt: Salesforce's relationship fields are fundamentally one-to-many. How do you model a true many-to-many relationship -- say, Students who can each attend many Courses, and Courses with many Students?
questions.modelAnswer: Salesforce's lookup and master-detail relationship fields are inherently one-to-many -- a single relationship field on one object can only point at one record on the other side. A true many-to-many relationship, like Students and Courses, is modeled with a junction object sitting between the two: a new custom object, often called something like Enrollment, that has two master-detail (or lookup) relationship fields, one to Student and one to Course. Each Enrollment record represents a single student-in-a-course pairing, so a student with three Enrollment records is effectively linked to three different Courses, and a Course with many Enrollment records is linked to many different Students, without either Student or Course ever needing a direct many-to-many field that the platform doesn't support.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw it out as a middle table: Student and Course never talk to each other directly, because Salesforce doesn't give you a native many-to-many field. Instead I create an Enrollment object with a master-detail to Student and a master-detail to Course. Every time a student enrolls in a course, that's one new Enrollment record -- so if the student takes four courses, there are four Enrollment records, each linking that one student to one course. It's the same pattern as a classic join table in relational database design, Salesforce just calls it a junction object.
commonMistakes: Trying to use a single lookup or master-detail field to represent a many-to-many relationship directly
Not recognizing the junction object pattern as equivalent to a relational database join table
Forgetting the junction object needs two relationship fields, one to each side
Choosing lookup when master-detail (or vice versa) better fits the cascading/security needs of the scenario
keyPoints: Salesforce relationship fields are inherently one-to-many, not many-to-many
A junction object sits between the two objects with a relationship field to each
Each junction record represents one specific pairing between the two sides
This mirrors the classic join-table pattern from relational database design

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why a junction object is needed
Correctly describes how the junction object is structured
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: The Modern Data Stack, in Plain Terms
questions.prompt: You keep hearing terms like Snowflake, dbt, and Airflow mentioned alongside Salesforce data work. At a beginner level, what does each one roughly do, and how do they typically fit together?
questions.modelAnswer: Snowflake is a cloud data warehouse -- a place to store and query very large volumes of structured data, separate from any single application like Salesforce, with compute and storage scaled independently. dbt (data build tool) is a transformation layer that runs inside the warehouse, letting analysts write SQL-based models that turn raw, loaded data into clean, business-ready tables, with built-in testing and documentation. Airflow is an orchestration tool that schedules and sequences jobs -- for example, running the extraction of Salesforce data into Snowflake first, then triggering the dbt transformation models afterward, then kicking off a downstream report refresh -- making sure each step runs in the right order, on the right schedule, and alerts someone if a step fails. Together, a typical flow is: data lands in Snowflake, dbt transforms it into usable models, and Airflow orchestrates when each of those steps runs.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the three as answering three different questions. Snowflake answers 'where does the data live once it's out of Salesforce and ready for heavy analysis.' dbt answers 'how do we turn the raw, messy loaded data into clean tables people can actually trust and query.' Airflow answers 'what order do all these jobs run in, and on what schedule, and who gets alerted if something breaks.' A simple version of the pipeline I'd picture: Airflow kicks off a job that pulls Salesforce data into Snowflake, waits for that to finish, then kicks off the dbt models that clean and reshape it, and finally triggers whatever depends on the finished tables. None of the three do the other two jobs -- they're genuinely complementary pieces of the same pipeline.
commonMistakes: Describing Snowflake, dbt, and Airflow as competing or interchangeable tools
Not knowing dbt is specifically a transformation layer, not a storage or orchestration tool
Confusing Airflow's scheduling/orchestration role with dbt's transformation role
Missing how the three tools typically chain together in a real pipeline
keyPoints: Snowflake is a cloud data warehouse for storing and querying large volumes of data
dbt is a SQL-based transformation layer that builds clean, tested models inside the warehouse
Airflow orchestrates and schedules the order in which pipeline jobs run
A typical pipeline loads data into Snowflake, transforms it with dbt, and is sequenced by Airflow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes what each of the three tools does
Correctly explains how they typically fit together
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: What Data Governance Means in an Enterprise Salesforce Org
questions.prompt: What does 'data governance' actually mean in the context of an enterprise Salesforce org, beyond just having good security settings?
questions.modelAnswer: Data governance is the set of policies, processes, and ownership assignments that determine who is accountable for a given piece of data's quality, definition, and lifecycle -- not just who technically has access to it. In an enterprise Salesforce org that goes beyond security, governance covers things like: a single, agreed-upon definition of what a field like 'Active Customer' means so different teams aren't silently using different definitions; data quality standards and ownership for who's responsible for fixing bad data in a given object; retention and archival policies for old records; and change management for who can approve a new field or object being added so the data model doesn't sprawl uncontrolled. Security (who can see or edit a record) is one piece of governance, but governance is the broader discipline of making data trustworthy and consistently understood across the whole organization, not just locked down.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd draw the line this way: security answers 'who's allowed to see or touch this data,' and governance answers a much bigger set of questions -- who owns this field's definition, what happens to this record after it's five years old, who has to approve a new custom object before it ships, and whose job it is when a report's numbers look wrong because two teams built it on different assumptions about what a field means. Security is a piece of governance, but it's definitely not all of it. In a growing enterprise org, the real governance pain usually isn't someone seeing data they shouldn't -- it's three different teams each having their own private definition of 'Active Customer' and nobody noticing until the numbers in two dashboards don't match.
commonMistakes: Equating data governance entirely with security and access control
Not mentioning data definitions and consistency as a governance concern
Missing retention/lifecycle policy as part of governance
Not identifying ownership and change-approval as governance responsibilities
keyPoints: Governance is broader than security -- it covers ownership, definitions, quality, and lifecycle
A shared, agreed definition of key fields/metrics prevents silent inconsistency across teams
Retention and archival policy is a governance concern, not just a technical one
Change management for new fields/objects is part of keeping the data model trustworthy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes governance from pure security
Gives concrete, accurate examples of governance concerns

questions.title: Writing a Basic Apex Trigger Skeleton
questions.prompt: Write a simple Apex trigger on the Opportunity object that runs before a record is inserted or updated, and sets a custom field Priority_Flag__c to true whenever the Amount field is over 100000.
questions.modelAnswer: A before-insert/before-update trigger is the right event choice here because the logic only sets a field on the same record being saved -- there's no need for an after-save context or a second DML statement. The trigger iterates Trigger.new (the in-memory, about-to-be-saved versions of the records), checks Amount with a null guard since Amount can be blank, and sets Priority_Flag__c directly on each record in the loop -- because it's a before trigger, those field changes are automatically included in the same save with no extra DML required.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd default straight to a before trigger here, not after, because I'm only touching a field on the record that's already in memory about to be saved -- no need to trigger a second save. I always loop over Trigger.new rather than query anything, since Trigger.new already has every record and field I need. The one thing I'm careful about is the null check on Amount, since a blank Amount would throw a null pointer exception on the comparison if I didn't guard for it.
questions.example: A new Opportunity saved with Amount = 150000 gets Priority_Flag__c automatically set to true before the insert completes, with no second DML statement needed.
commonMistakes: Using an after-insert/after-update trigger for same-record-only logic, forcing an unnecessary second DML
Forgetting the null check on Amount, causing a runtime exception on blank values
Querying the Opportunity records again inside the trigger instead of using Trigger.new directly
Not handling both insert and update, missing records that cross the threshold on an edit
keyPoints: Before-trigger context is correct for same-record-only field updates
Trigger.new holds the in-memory records about to be saved
A null guard on Amount prevents a runtime exception
Setting the field directly in a before trigger avoids a second DML statement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct trigger event (before insert/update)
Correct logic and null handling
Explains why before-trigger avoids extra DML

questions.title: Fixing a SOQL-in-a-Loop Anti-Pattern
questions.modelAnswer: The original code issues one SOQL query and one DML update per account in the list, which will throw 'Too many SOQL queries: 101' or 'Too many DML statements: 151' once the list gets large enough -- both are classic non-bulkified anti-patterns. The fix moves the query outside the loop entirely, using a single SOQL query with a WHERE Id IN :accountIds clause to fetch every relevant Account in one call, then collects the ones that need updating into a List<Account>, and issues exactly one update DML statement on that list at the end, regardless of how many accounts are being processed.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway here is a SELECT and an update both sitting inside a for loop -- that's going to blow past limits the moment this runs on more than 100 or so accounts, which it will in a bulk context like a batch job or a list-view mass action. My fix is always the same shape: query once, up front, for everything I need with an IN clause, collect whatever needs changing into a list as I iterate, and do exactly one DML call at the very end on that whole list. It reads almost the same, it's just restructured so the number of queries and DML calls stays constant no matter how many records come in.
commonMistakes: Leaving the SOQL query inside the loop even after moving the DML outside
Forgetting to add Rating to the SELECT fields even though it isn't filtered on, just updated
Not checking whether the update list is empty before calling update, which still works but is a lazy habit
Using a WHERE Id = :accId single-record query pattern instead of a bulk IN clause
keyPoints: SOQL and DML inside a loop don't scale and trigger governor limit exceptions
Query once outside the loop using WHERE Id IN :collection
Collect records needing changes into a list while iterating
Issue exactly one DML statement on the collected list after the loop

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly moves SOQL query outside the loop with an IN clause
Correctly moves DML outside the loop into a single bulk statement
Explains why the original pattern fails at scale

questions.title: Building a Minimal Lightning Web Component
questions.prompt: Write the JavaScript and HTML for a minimal LWC that displays a greeting message passed in from a parent component via a public property called greeting.
questions.modelAnswer: The @api decorator on the greeting property is what exposes it as a public attribute a parent component can set, like <c-greeting-display greeting="Hello"></c-greeting-display>. The HTML template simply binds to {greeting} inside curly braces, which LWC's reactive rendering keeps in sync automatically whenever the parent updates the value -- no manual DOM manipulation or re-render call is needed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out the one decorator that makes this work: @api. Without it, greeting would just be a private, internal property the component can't receive from the outside. With @api on it, a parent component can pass a value straight into the attribute, same spelling, camelCase in JS and kebab-case in the markup. The template side is about as simple as LWC gets -- just drop the property name in curly braces and the framework's own reactivity handles re-rendering it whenever the value changes, I don't have to wire that up myself.
questions.example: Parent usage: <c-greeting-display greeting="Welcome back, Jordan"></c-greeting-display> renders 'Welcome back, Jordan' inside the child component.

Mixing up camelCase JS property names with kebab-case HTML attribute names
Trying to manually trigger a re-render instead of relying on LWC's built-in reactivity
Importing from the wrong module path instead of 'lwc'

questions.title: Spinning Up a Scratch Org with Salesforce CLI
questions.prompt: Walk through the Salesforce CLI (sf) commands to create a new scratch org from an existing project's scratch org definition file, push source to it, and open it in the browser.
questions.code:
sf org create scratch --definition-file config/project-scratch-def.json --alias my-scratch --set-default --duration-days 7

sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app

sf org open
questions.modelAnswer: The first command creates the scratch org itself from the project's scratch org definition JSON file, gives it a friendly alias, sets it as the default org for subsequent commands, and sets how many days it will live before expiring. The second command pushes (deploys) the project's local source metadata into that newly created, empty scratch org, since a fresh scratch org starts with no custom metadata at all -- just the base org shape defined in the definition file. The third command opens the scratch org directly in a browser tab, authenticated automatically using the CLI's stored credentials, with no manual login needed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it exactly in that order, because each step depends on the last one existing. First I create the scratch org pointing at the project's own definition file -- that file is what decides things like which features and editions the org gets -- and I always set an alias so I'm not referring to it by some generated username later. Second, the scratch org is empty right after creation, so I deploy my local source into it; this is the step that actually puts my Apex classes, LWCs, and custom objects into the org. Third, opening it is just a convenience -- the CLI already has the auth token stored from creation, so it logs me straight in without typing a password.

Forgetting the scratch org starts empty and skipping the deploy/push step entirely
Not setting an alias, making later commands harder to target the right org
Assuming scratch orgs persist indefinitely instead of expiring after the set duration

questions.title: Creating a Named Credential for an External Callout
questions.prompt: You need an Apex callout to a partner's REST API that requires an API key in a header. Walk through creating a Named Credential so the endpoint URL and the key aren't hardcoded in Apex.
questions.modelAnswer: A Named Credential stores an external endpoint's URL and its authentication details (like an API key, OAuth settings, or a username/password) as a reusable, admin-managed setting, so Apex code references the credential by name instead of hardcoding the endpoint or secret directly. From Setup, Named Credentials, create a new one: specify the external system's base URL, choose the authentication type (for a simple API key scenario, this is often set up alongside a custom header via an Auth. Provider or, more simply, with the key embedded via a Named Credential's custom header configuration), and save. In Apex, the callout then targets 'callout:MyNamedCredential/some/path' instead of a literal URL string, and the platform automatically attaches the configured authentication to the HTTP request.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd never hardcode an endpoint URL or an API key directly into an Apex class -- that's a security and maintainability problem the moment the key needs to rotate or the endpoint changes. So I go to Setup, Named Credentials, create a new one, give it a clear name, and point it at the partner's base URL. I configure the authentication there too, so the key itself lives in a protected setting, not in code. Back in Apex, instead of building the full URL and setting an Authorization header manually, I just call out to 'callout:PartnerAPI/orders' and the platform handles attaching whatever credentials I configured -- so if the key ever needs to rotate, I update it in one place in Setup, and no Apex code or deployment is required.

questions.title: Testing a Salesforce REST API Call with a Tool Like Workbench
questions.prompt: Before writing any integration code, you want to confirm a simple GET request to the Salesforce REST API for Account records actually works and returns what you expect. Walk through doing that with a tool like Workbench or Postman.
questions.modelAnswer: First you need a valid session -- Workbench authenticates directly against the org via OAuth login, while Postman typically needs an access token obtained via a Connected App's OAuth flow. Once authenticated, you issue a GET request to a REST endpoint such as /services/data/v59.0/query/?q=SELECT+Id,Name+FROM+Account+LIMIT+5 (a SOQL query over REST), with the session's access token sent as an Authorization: Bearer header. The response comes back as JSON, including a 'records' array with the queried fields and a 'totalSize' count, which confirms the endpoint, query, and authentication are all working correctly before any real Apex or external integration code is written against it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always test the raw call before I write a single line of integration code, because it isolates whether a problem is the API itself or my code around it. In Workbench, that's simple -- it logs me in directly and I can just hit the REST Explorer with a GET to the query endpoint, with my SOQL URL-encoded in the query string. In Postman, I'd first need to get an OAuth token from a Connected App, then set that as a Bearer token in the Authorization header for the GET request. Either way, if I get back clean JSON with a records array and the right field values, I know the query and the credentials are both solid, and any bugs after that are in the integration code I write, not the API call itself.

Not setting the Authorization: Bearer header correctly in a tool like Postman
Confusing the REST query endpoint's JSON response shape with SOAP API's XML response

The REST query endpoint accepts a URL-encoded SOQL query string
The Authorization: Bearer header carries the session token

questions.title: Writing a Basic SOQL Query with a Relationship Filter
questions.prompt: Write a SOQL query that returns the Name and Email of every Contact whose related Account's Industry is 'Technology', ordered by the Contact's LastName.
questions.code:
SELECT Name, Email
FROM Contact
WHERE Account.Industry = 'Technology'
ORDER BY LastName ASC
questions.modelAnswer: This is a child-to-parent relationship query -- Contact is the child, Account is the parent, and dot notation (Account.Industry) lets you filter on a field from the related parent record directly in the WHERE clause without a separate query or a join keyword, since SOQL doesn't use JOIN syntax the way SQL does. Ordering by LastName sorts the result set alphabetically by the Contact's last name, which is a straightforward field on the Contact object itself rather than the related Account.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out the thing that trips up people coming from plain SQL: there's no JOIN keyword in SOQL. To reach up to the parent Account's Industry field from a Contact query, you just use dot notation, Account.Industry, right in the WHERE clause, and SOQL resolves that relationship automatically because Account is Contact's standard parent lookup. ORDER BY LastName at the end is just sorting on a normal field on the Contact record itself -- no relationship traversal needed there at all.
commonMistakes: Trying to write a JOIN clause, which doesn't exist in SOQL syntax
Forgetting dot notation is required to reach a parent object's field from a child query
Ordering by the wrong object's field or forgetting ORDER BY entirely
Using child-to-parent dot notation when the relationship actually runs the other direction
keyPoints: SOQL has no JOIN keyword; parent fields are reached via dot notation
Account.Industry filters on the related parent Account's field from a Contact query
ORDER BY sorts on a field of the queried object itself
This is a child-to-parent relationship traversal (Contact to Account)

Correct WHERE clause with dot-notation relationship filter
Correct ORDER BY clause

questions.title: Writing a SOQL Aggregate Query
questions.prompt: Write a SOQL query that returns the total Amount and the count of Opportunities, grouped by StageName, but only for Opportunities with an Amount greater than zero.
questions.code:
SELECT StageName, SUM(Amount) totalAmount, COUNT(Id) oppCount
FROM Opportunity
WHERE Amount > 0
GROUP BY StageName
questions.modelAnswer: This uses two SOQL aggregate functions, SUM and COUNT, alongside a GROUP BY clause on StageName -- the aggregate functions calculate across all rows within each distinct StageName bucket rather than returning individual record rows. The WHERE Amount > 0 filter is applied before the grouping and aggregation happen, excluding any Opportunity with a blank or zero Amount from the totals entirely. In Apex, a query like this returns a List<AggregateResult> rather than a List<Opportunity>, since the shape of the result is summary rows, not full sObject records.
questions.professionalAnswer: The two things I'd flag here: first, SUM and COUNT are aggregate functions, and the moment you use one alongside a GROUP BY, you're no longer getting back individual Opportunity records -- you get one summary row per distinct StageName value. Second, the WHERE clause filters rows before they're grouped and summed, so any Opportunity with Amount at zero or null just doesn't make it into any bucket's total at all. If I were consuming this in Apex, I'd remember the return type is List<AggregateResult>, not List<Opportunity>, and I'd access the aliased fields like totalAmount and oppCount rather than trying to read them as standard Opportunity fields.
commonMistakes: Forgetting GROUP BY is required when mixing aggregate functions with a non-aggregated field like StageName
Not aliasing the aggregate fields, making them harder to reference in Apex
Placing the Amount filter after grouping instead of in a WHERE clause before it
Assuming the Apex return type is List<Opportunity> instead of List<AggregateResult>
keyPoints: SUM and COUNT are aggregate functions that summarize across grouped rows
GROUP BY StageName produces one summary row per distinct stage
WHERE filters rows before aggregation happens
Aggregate SOQL in Apex returns List<AggregateResult>, not sObject records

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct use of SUM and COUNT
Correct GROUP BY clause
Correct WHERE clause placement/filter

questions.title: Writing a SOSL Search Across Multiple Objects
questions.prompt: Write a SOSL query that searches for the term 'Acme' across Account Name, Contact Name, and Lead Company/Name fields, returning the Id and Name (or Company, for Leads) from each matching object.
questions.code:
FIND {Acme} IN ALL FIELDS
RETURNING Account(Id, Name), Contact(Id, Name), Lead(Id, Name, Company)
questions.modelAnswer: FIND specifies the search term, IN ALL FIELDS tells SOSL to search across every searchable field rather than restricting to a specific field group like NAME FIELDS, and RETURNING lists each object type to search along with the specific fields to return for matches on that object -- here Account and Contact return Id and Name, while Lead also returns Company since that's often the more meaningful identifier for an unconverted Lead. SOSL returns a list of lists (one list per RETURNING object type), in the same order the objects were listed in the RETURNING clause, which matters when parsing the result in Apex.
questions.professionalAnswer: The structure I always keep in mind with SOSL is FIND, then where to search, then RETURNING, where I explicitly list every object type I want searched along with exactly which fields I want back for each one. I used IN ALL FIELDS here instead of NAME FIELDS because the term could plausibly show up in more than just a name field, though if I wanted to be more targeted and faster, NAME FIELDS would narrow the search appropriately. One thing I'd flag for whoever's consuming this in Apex: the result comes back as a List<List<sObject>>, with each inner list corresponding to one of the RETURNING object types in the order they were written, so Account results, Contact results, and Lead results are three separate lists, not one combined list.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the RETURNING clause, which is required to specify fields per object type
Using NAME FIELDS when the search genuinely needs to cover more than just name fields, or vice versa
Not knowing SOSL returns a List<List<sObject>> structure in Apex, one list per returning object
Omitting Company for Lead when Name alone may not be populated on an unconverted Lead
keyPoints: FIND specifies the search term; RETURNING specifies which objects and fields to return
IN ALL FIELDS searches broadly; NAME FIELDS narrows to name-type fields only
SOSL searches multiple objects in a single query, unlike SOQL
Apex receives the result as a List<List<sObject>>, ordered by the RETURNING clause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct FIND and search scope clause
Correct RETURNING clause with all three objects and appropriate fields
Explains the Apex result shape correctly

questions.title: Building a Basic CRM Analytics Dataset from a Dataflow
questions.prompt: Walk through the basic steps to get Opportunity data from Salesforce into a usable CRM Analytics dataset so it can be explored in a lens or dashboard.
questions.modelAnswer: In CRM Analytics, you create or edit a dataflow (or the newer Recipe-based equivalent) that defines a digest node pulling the Opportunity object and the specific fields needed, runs any needed transformation steps (joins, filters, computed fields), and ends with a 'register dataset' step that outputs the result as a named, queryable CRM Analytics dataset. Running the dataflow (either manually or on a schedule) processes the data through those steps and makes the resulting dataset available for exploration. Once registered, that dataset can be opened in a lens to explore interactively or used as the data source for a dashboard widget.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it as a pipeline, not a single click: first I build or edit a dataflow, starting with a digest node that pulls Opportunity and whatever fields I actually need -- I don't just grab everything, since that bloats the dataset. If I need to shape the data, I add transformation nodes, maybe a join to bring in Account fields or a filter to drop closed-lost records I don't care about. The critical last step is the register step, which is what actually turns the processed output into a named dataset CRM Analytics can query -- skip that and the data never becomes usable in a lens or dashboard. Then I run the dataflow, either by hand to test it or on a schedule for ongoing refreshes, and once it finishes successfully, the dataset shows up and I can open a lens straight on it.

questions.title: Writing a Basic dbt Staging Model
questions.prompt: Write a minimal dbt model file that stages a raw Salesforce Opportunity source table, renaming a couple of columns and casting Amount to a numeric type, following the staging-layer convention of doing only light cleanup with no business logic.
questions.code:
-- models/staging/stg_salesforce__opportunities.sql
select
    id as opportunity_id,
    name as opportunity_name,
    stagename as stage_name,
    cast(amount as numeric) as amount,
    closedate as close_date
from {{ source('salesforce', 'opportunity') }}
questions.modelAnswer: This is a staging model, which by convention stays close to a 1:1 mapping with the raw source table -- it only renames columns to clearer, consistent names (id to opportunity_id, stagename to stage_name) and casts Amount to a proper numeric type, with no joins, no business logic, and no filtering beyond basic cleanup. The {{ source('salesforce', 'opportunity') }} function references a source defined in dbt's sources YAML configuration rather than hardcoding a raw table name, which keeps the model resilient if the underlying schema or database location changes. Keeping staging models this light is what allows every downstream model to build on a clean, consistently named foundation instead of each analyst re-deriving naming conventions independently.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep this deliberately boring, because that's the whole point of a staging model -- rename things to a consistent, readable naming convention, cast types where the raw source has them wrong (Amount often lands as text or an imprecise type depending on the extraction tool), and stop there. No business logic, no joins to other tables, nothing clever. I use the source() function instead of hardcoding the raw table's name, so if the raw data ever moves to a different schema, I only update the sources YAML file once instead of hunting through every model that references it. Any real business logic -- like defining what counts as a 'closed-won deal' -- belongs one layer up, in an intermediate model, not here.

Skipping the type cast on Amount, leaving it as whatever type the raw load produced
Not following a consistent renaming convention across staging models

The source() function references a configured source instead of a hardcoded table name
Type casting belongs in staging so downstream models can trust the column types
Business logic belongs in later layers (intermediate/marts), not staging

Correct use of source() instead of a hardcoded table
