questions.title: Diagnosing 'Too Many SOQL Queries: 101'
questions.prompt: A batch update script works fine on 10 test records but throws 'System.LimitException: Too many SOQL queries: 101' when run against a few hundred records. What's actually happening, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This error means a SOQL query is being executed inside a loop, so the number of queries scales directly with the number of records processed -- with 10 records it stayed under the 100-query ceiling, but a few hundred records pushes well past it. The fix is to move the query outside the loop entirely: query once for every relevant record up front using a WHERE Id IN :collection clause (or an equivalent bulk-safe pattern), build any needed lookup structures (like a Map<Id, SObject>) from that single query's results, and reference the map inside the loop instead of issuing a fresh query per iteration.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I see this error, I already know roughly what I'm going to find before I even open the code -- a SELECT statement sitting inside a for loop somewhere. It passed at 10 records purely by luck, because 10 queries is nowhere near the 100 limit, but the failure scales linearly with record count, so it was always going to break eventually. My fix is always the same pattern: pull the query out, run it once with an IN clause covering every ID I need, stuff the results into a map keyed by Id, and then the loop just does a map lookup instead of a fresh query each time. I'd also double check there isn't a second query hiding somewhere else in a helper method being called from inside that same loop, since that's an easy way to miss the real source.
commonMistakes: Assuming the error means the governor limit itself is too low rather than that the code isn't bulk-safe
Fixing the query in the obvious loop but missing a second query hidden in a called helper method
Adding a LIMIT clause to the inner query instead of restructuring to avoid querying in the loop at all
Not using a Map<Id, SObject> to look up results efficiently after moving the query outside the loop
keyPoints: The error means a SOQL query runs once per loop iteration, scaling with record count
Passing on a small test set and failing at scale is the classic symptom of this anti-pattern
The fix moves the query outside the loop with a single bulk query using WHERE Id IN :collection
Results should be stored in a map for fast lookup inside the loop afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the SOQL-in-loop root cause
Correctly describes the fix (bulk query + map lookup)
Mentions checking for hidden queries in called methods

questions.title: Trigger Recursion Causing Duplicate Processing
questions.prompt: An after-update trigger on Case updates a related Account field, but that Account update somehow triggers the same Case logic to run again, and support agents are seeing duplicate email notifications. What's going on, and how would you prevent it?
questions.modelAnswer: This is trigger recursion: the Case trigger's after-update logic performs DML on the Account, and something on the Account side (a workflow rule, another trigger, or a flow) updates a field back on the related Case, which re-fires the original Case trigger and repeats the whole sequence, including sending another notification email. The standard fix is a recursion guard -- a static Boolean variable (static so it persists for the duration of the single transaction) that's checked and set at the top of the trigger logic, so the second time the trigger fires within the same transaction, the guard short-circuits the logic before it runs again and re-sends the email.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the classic symptom of a trigger that updates something, and that something updates back, and now you're in a loop within a single transaction. I'd trace the chain first -- Case trigger updates Account, so what on the Account side is writing back to the Case? Once I find that piece (often a workflow rule or another trigger nobody remembered was there), the actual fix I reach for is a static recursion-guard variable at the top of the Apex class: check if it's already true, and if so, skip the logic entirely; if not, set it true before doing the work. Because static variables live for the whole transaction, not just one trigger invocation, that guard reliably stops the second pass from re-sending the notification, without needing to touch or remove whatever's on the Account side causing the write-back.
commonMistakes: Trying to fix it only by modifying the Account-side automation instead of guarding the Case trigger itself
Using an instance variable instead of a static variable for the recursion guard, which won't persist correctly
Not tracing the actual write-back chain before attempting a fix
Assuming the duplicate email is a Flow/Apex email bug rather than the trigger genuinely firing twice
keyPoints: Recursion happens when a trigger's own DML indirectly causes it to fire again in the same transaction
Tracing the write-back chain (what on the Account side updates the Case) is the first diagnostic step
A static Boolean recursion guard, checked and set at the top of the trigger logic, is the standard fix
Static variables persist for the whole transaction, which is why they work for this guard

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the recursion mechanism
Correctly describes the static recursion-guard fix
Mentions tracing the actual write-back chain

questions.title: An LWC's @wire Property Comes Back Undefined
questions.prompt: An LWC uses @wire(getRecord, {...}) to pull Account fields, but the component's data property is undefined on initial render, causing a null-reference error elsewhere in the JavaScript. What's the likely cause, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: A @wire adapter like getRecord is asynchronous -- the component renders immediately while the actual data request is still in flight, so on the very first render, the wired property is genuinely undefined until the server responds; code that assumes it's populated immediately will throw a null-reference error. The fix is to guard any logic that depends on the wired data with a null/undefined check (or use the template's conditional directives, like if:true, to only render dependent markup once data has arrived), and to use the wire adapter's error parameter alongside data so both the loading and error states are explicitly handled instead of assumed away.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing to remember about @wire is it's reactive and asynchronous -- the component mounts and renders before the data has actually come back from the server, so of course that property is undefined for a beat. My fix is never to assume it's populated; I check for it explicitly, either in the JS getter logic or directly in the template with an if:true directive, so nothing tries to read a field off an object that hasn't arrived yet. I also always destructure both data and error from the wire result, because if I only handle data, a genuine fetch failure just silently leaves things undefined forever with no feedback to the user, which looks identical to 'still loading' from the UI's perspective.
commonMistakes: Assuming @wire data is available synchronously on first render
Not guarding template or JS logic against the data property being undefined initially
Only destructuring data from the wire result and ignoring the error parameter
Confusing a genuine fetch error with the normal, brief undefined state before data arrives
keyPoints: @wire adapters are asynchronous; data is undefined until the response arrives
Logic depending on wired data needs explicit null/undefined guards
Template conditional directives can defer rendering until data exists
Both data and error should be handled, not just data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the asynchronous nature of @wire as the root cause
Correctly describes the guard/conditional-rendering fix
Mentions handling the error parameter as well

questions.title: An Apex Callout Fails Silently with an Unhandled Exception
questions.prompt: An Apex method makes an HTTP callout to an external system, and when that system is slow or returns an error, the whole Apex transaction fails with an unhandled exception and the user sees a generic error page. How would you fix this so it fails gracefully?
questions.modelAnswer: The callout code is almost certainly missing a try/catch block and isn't checking the HTTP response status code, so any network timeout, non-2xx response, or malformed response throws (or should be checked for and explicitly handled) rather than letting the exception propagate all the way up to a generic error page. The fix wraps the callout in a try/catch for CalloutException (and any other relevant exception types), checks res.getStatusCode() after a successful call to confirm it's actually a success range code rather than a 4xx/5xx error body, and returns a clear, specific, user-facing message (or logs the failure and shows a friendly fallback) instead of letting the raw exception surface to the end user.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd check is whether there's a try/catch around the callout at all -- a lot of first-draft callout code just assumes success. I'd wrap it in a try/catch for CalloutException specifically, since that's what Apex throws for network-level failures like timeouts, and separately check the response's status code even when the call technically succeeds at the network level, because a 500 error from the partner system still comes back as a normal HttpResponse object, not an exception -- it just has a bad status code I have to check for myself. Once I catch the failure, I don't let the raw exception message bubble up to the user; I log the real details somewhere useful for debugging and show something clear and specific instead of a generic error page.
commonMistakes: Not wrapping the callout in a try/catch for CalloutException
Assuming a non-exception response means success without checking the status code
Letting the raw exception message surface directly to the end user
Not distinguishing between a network-level failure and an application-level error response
keyPoints: CalloutException should be caught explicitly around the HTTP call
A successful HTTP call can still return a non-2xx status code that must be checked separately
Error details should be logged, not shown raw to the end user
A friendly, specific fallback message improves on a generic error page

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the missing try/catch and status-code check
Correctly describes graceful failure handling for the user
Distinguishes network-level failure from application-level error response

questions.title: A Deployment Fails Between Sandboxes with a Missing Dependency Error
questions.prompt: You're deploying a change set (or a source-based deployment) from one sandbox to another, and it fails with an error about a missing field or component that 'does not exist' in the target. The component genuinely exists in your source org. What's the likely cause, and how do you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This is almost always a missing dependency -- the component being deployed (say, a validation rule or a flow) references another component (a custom field, a record type, or a custom object) that exists in the source org but hasn't been deployed to the target org yet, so the target genuinely has no such component for the reference to resolve against. The fix is to identify every dependency of the component being deployed and include all of them in the same deployment, or deploy the missing prerequisite components first in a separate, earlier deployment, then deploy the dependent component afterward once its dependencies already exist in the target.
questions.professionalAnswer: Nine times out of ten when I see 'this field doesn't exist' on a deployment and I know for a fact it exists in my source org, it's because something that component depends on hasn't made the trip to the target org yet -- the component itself might be fine, but one of its dependencies got left behind. My fix is to actually map out what the failing component references -- a lookup to a custom object, a reference to a record type, whatever it is -- and either bundle every one of those dependencies into the same deployment, or deploy them in a deliberate order: prerequisites first, in their own deployment, and only then the component that depends on them. Change sets in particular are notorious for not always auto-including every dependency, so I don't trust the 'add dependencies' button blindly; I double check the list myself.
commonMistakes: Assuming the component itself is broken rather than looking for a missing dependency
Trusting a change set's automatic 'add dependencies' feature without manually verifying the list
Deploying everything in one unordered batch instead of deploying prerequisites first when needed
Not checking whether a referenced record type, field, or object even exists yet in the target org
keyPoints: The error usually means a dependency of the deployed component is missing in the target org
Dependencies (fields, record types, related objects) must exist in the target before the dependent component
A deployment can either bundle all dependencies together or deploy prerequisites first
Change sets don't always reliably auto-include every dependency

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the missing-dependency cause
Correctly describes the fix (bundle or sequence dependencies)
Notes change sets don't always auto-include dependencies reliably

questions.title: A SOQL Query Returns Zero Rows When Records Clearly Exist
questions.prompt: This query returns zero rows, even though you can see matching records in the UI: SELECT Id FROM Lead WHERE Email = 'John.Smith@Example.com' AND Status != 'Converted'. What are the likely causes, and how would you fix the query?
questions.code:
SELECT Id, Email, Status, ConvertedDate, IsConverted
FROM Lead
WHERE Email = 'John.Smith@Example.com'
questions.modelAnswer: Two likely causes stack up here. First, Status != 'Converted' excludes records where Status is null -- SOQL's inequality operator doesn't match null values the way some developers expect, so if any matching Lead has a blank Status, it's silently excluded. Second, and more specifically for converted Leads, Salesforce actually blanks out the Status field (or it becomes less meaningful) on conversion in some configurations, and the more reliable way to check conversion state is the dedicated IsConverted boolean field, not a Status text comparison. The fix is to drop the speculative filter first, run a broader diagnostic query like the one shown to see what's actually there, and then rebuild the real filter using IsConverted = false instead of a fragile Status string comparison.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move whenever a filtered query returns nothing I'm sure should be there is to strip the filters back and just query the record directly on the field I'm sure is right -- in this case just Email, with no Status condition at all -- to see what's actually on the record. That usually reveals the real issue fast: either Status is null (which != 'Converted' silently excludes, since SOQL doesn't treat null as 'not equal' the way you'd hope), or the Lead actually is converted and its Status field doesn't hold the value I assumed. Once I see the real data, I'd rebuild the filter using the purpose-built IsConverted boolean field instead of trying to infer conversion state from a text Status value, which is a much more fragile thing to filter on in the first place.
commonMistakes: Not knowing SOQL's != operator excludes null values rather than matching them
Filtering on Status text to determine conversion state instead of using IsConverted
Not stripping filters down to diagnose what data actually exists before assuming a tooling bug
Assuming case sensitivity is the problem when SOQL string equality is typically case-insensitive for standard text comparisons
keyPoints: != in SOQL does not match null values, silently excluding blank-field records
IsConverted is the reliable boolean field for checking Lead conversion state, not Status text
Stripping filters to a minimal diagnostic query reveals the real data before assuming a bug
Rebuilding the filter on the correct field fixes the root cause rather than patching symptoms

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the null-exclusion behavior of !=
Correctly identifies IsConverted as the right field to use
Describes a sound diagnostic approach (strip filters first)

questions.title: A SOQL Query Hits a Row Limit on a Large Object
questions.prompt: A report-generation script runs SELECT Id, Amount FROM Opportunity WHERE CreatedDate >= LAST_N_YEARS:2 with no LIMIT clause against an org with millions of Opportunities, and it times out or hits a query-result-size limit. How would you fix this?
questions.code:
SELECT Id, Amount FROM Opportunity
WHERE CreatedDate >= :startDate
ORDER BY Id
LIMIT 2000
questions.modelAnswer: Without a LIMIT, the query attempts to return every matching row in one pass, which against millions of records risks hitting the query result size limit or simply taking too long to process in a single synchronous transaction. The fix is to paginate: add an explicit LIMIT (commonly chosen to match a manageable batch size) plus a stable ORDER BY (typically on Id, which is unique and indexed) and track the last-seen value to filter the next batch with Id > :lastSeenId on subsequent calls -- or, better, hand this kind of large-scale processing to Batch Apex, which handles the chunking and governor-limit resets automatically instead of a hand-rolled pagination loop.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway here is 'millions of records' and no LIMIT in sight -- that query is trying to pull back everything that matches in a single shot, and at that scale it's going to run into either a timeout or the platform's own result-size ceiling before it finishes. If this really needs to run as one script, I'd paginate it manually: order by Id, limit each batch to something reasonable like 2000, and track the last Id I saw so the next query picks up with Id greater than that. But honestly, the real fix for 'process millions of records' almost always is Batch Apex instead of a loop of manual SOQL pages -- it's built exactly for this, chunking the work and giving each chunk a fresh set of governor limits automatically, instead of me reinventing that logic by hand.
commonMistakes: Running an unbounded query against a very large object with no LIMIT or pagination strategy
Pagination without a stable, unique ORDER BY, risking skipped or duplicated rows between pages
Not considering Batch Apex as the purpose-built tool for large-scale record processing
Assuming a single synchronous transaction can safely process millions of rows at once
keyPoints: Unbounded queries against very large objects risk timeouts or result-size limits
Pagination needs a LIMIT plus a stable, unique ORDER BY (commonly Id)
Tracking the last-seen value lets the next page pick up where the last left off
Batch Apex is the purpose-built tool for processing large record volumes at scale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the unbounded-query problem
Correctly describes a sound pagination approach
Mentions Batch Apex as the better large-scale solution

questions.title: A CRM Analytics Dataset Isn't Reflecting Recent Salesforce Changes
questions.prompt: Users say a CRM Analytics dashboard is showing Opportunity data that's clearly out of date -- records closed last week still show as open. What's the likely cause, and what would you check first?
questions.modelAnswer: CRM Analytics datasets are a snapshot produced by running a dataflow (or recipe), not a live, real-time view of Salesforce data -- the dataset only reflects reality as of the last successful run. The most likely cause is that the dataflow's scheduled refresh either hasn't run recently, failed silently, or is scheduled less frequently than users expect. The first things to check are the dataflow's run history for failed or skipped jobs, the schedule's frequency and last successful completion time, and whether the dashboard's lens is actually pointed at the dataset that's supposed to be refreshing versus an older, orphaned one.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd remind everyone, including myself, is that a CRM Analytics dataset is not a live view -- it's a snapshot from the last time the dataflow successfully ran, so 'out of date' almost always means the refresh didn't happen the way everyone assumed. I'd go straight to the dataflow's run history and check two things: did it actually run on schedule, and did it finish successfully, or did it fail partway through without anyone noticing. I'd also double check the obvious-but-easy-to-miss possibility that the dashboard's lens is pointed at an old or duplicate dataset instead of the one that's actually being refreshed -- that happens more often than people expect after a dataset gets rebuilt or renamed.
commonMistakes: Assuming CRM Analytics datasets update in real time like a standard Salesforce report
Not checking the dataflow's run history for failed or skipped scheduled runs
Overlooking that a dashboard's lens might point at a stale or duplicate dataset
Jumping to rebuild the entire dataflow before confirming where the actual failure is
keyPoints: CRM Analytics datasets are snapshots from the last successful dataflow run, not live data
A failed or skipped scheduled run is the most common cause of stale data
Checking dataflow run history is the right first diagnostic step
A dashboard lens pointed at the wrong/stale dataset is an easy-to-miss alternate cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains datasets as periodic snapshots, not live data
Correctly identifies run-history/scheduling as the first check
Mentions the stale-lens-reference possibility

questions.title: Duplicate Rows from a Parent-to-Child Relationship Query
questions.prompt: A SOQL query selecting Opportunity fields along with a subquery on OpportunityLineItems is being flattened into a report in Apex, and the Opportunity's Amount appears to be counted multiple times -- once per line item. What's actually happening, and how do you fix the aggregation?
questions.code:
SELECT Id, Amount,
  (SELECT Id, Quantity, UnitPrice FROM OpportunityLineItems)
FROM Opportunity
WHERE Id = :oppId
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't actually a SOQL bug -- a parent-to-child subquery correctly returns one Opportunity record with a nested list of its related line items, so Amount itself isn't duplicated in the query result at all. The real issue is in how the Apex or reporting code consuming that result is iterating: if the code loops over each line item and, inside that loop, adds the parent Opportunity's Amount again for every line item, it's double (or triple) counting a single parent-level value once per child row. The fix is to read Amount once per Opportunity, outside any loop over its line items, and only loop over the line items for line-item-level fields like Quantity or UnitPrice.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd immediately suspect the consuming code rather than the query itself, because a parent-to-child subquery like this genuinely returns one Opportunity with a list of line items attached -- Amount lives once, at the parent level, no matter how many line items come back. The bug is almost certainly that whoever wrote the summing logic is looping over the line items and adding opp.Amount inside that same loop, which means a deal with four line items gets its Amount counted four times. The fix is just moving that Amount read outside the line-item loop -- grab it once per Opportunity, and only use the loop for things that are genuinely per-line-item, like Quantity times UnitPrice.
commonMistakes: Assuming the SOQL subquery itself is duplicating the parent's Amount field
Adding a parent-level field inside a loop meant only for child-level fields
Trying to deduplicate Amount after the fact instead of fixing where it's read in the loop
Not distinguishing parent-level totals from line-item-level values when designing the aggregation
keyPoints: A parent-to-child subquery correctly returns one parent record with a nested child list
Double-counting happens in the consuming code's loop, not in the SOQL query itself
Parent-level fields like Amount should be read once, outside any loop over child records
Line-item-level fields are the only values that should be summed inside the child loop

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly clears the SOQL query of blame and identifies the real cause
Correctly describes the fix (read parent field outside the loop)
Clearly distinguishes parent-level vs. child-level fields

questions.title: A dbt Model Breaks After an Upstream Schema Change
questions.prompt: A dbt model that worked fine for months suddenly fails to compile with a 'column does not exist' error, right after the Salesforce extraction job that feeds the raw source table was reconfigured. What's the likely cause, and how would you fix and prevent this?
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is that the upstream extraction job's reconfiguration changed a column name, dropped a field, or altered a data type in the raw source table, and the dbt model (likely a staging model) still references the old column name directly, so it fails to compile against the new schema. The immediate fix is to update the model's column references to match the new raw schema. To prevent this going forward, source freshness tests and schema tests (like checking expected columns exist) should run as part of CI against the raw source, so a breaking upstream change is caught by an automated test failure before it silently breaks downstream models in production.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is to actually diff the raw table's current schema against what the model expects -- almost certainly the extraction reconfiguration either renamed a column or changed its type, and the staging model is still pointing at the old name. The immediate fix is just updating that reference to match the new schema. But the real fix is making sure this doesn't quietly happen again: I'd add schema tests on the source definition that check the expected columns actually exist, and run those as part of CI so a reconfigured extraction job that breaks the schema fails a test and gets caught before it ever reaches a production model, instead of someone discovering it days later because a dashboard looks wrong.
commonMistakes: Assuming the dbt model itself has a bug rather than checking the upstream source schema first
Fixing the immediate column reference without adding any test to catch a repeat occurrence
Not knowing dbt source/schema tests can catch this kind of breaking change proactively
Not connecting the timing of the extraction reconfiguration to the failure at all
keyPoints: An upstream extraction schema change (renamed/dropped column, changed type) is the likely root cause
The immediate fix is updating the model's column references to the new schema
Schema/source tests in CI can catch a breaking upstream change before it reaches production models
Correlating the timing of the upstream change with the failure is a key diagnostic step

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the upstream schema change as the root cause
Correctly describes the immediate fix
Describes a sound prevention mechanism (schema tests in CI)

questions.title: System Design: Deciding Between Flow and Apex for a New Requirement
questions.prompt: A product team asks for a new piece of logic on Opportunity: when an Opportunity closes as Won, update three related records across two different objects, send a notification, and, for a specific subset of deal types, run a calculation involving a loop over an unrelated list of pricing tiers. As the person deciding how to build this, walk through how you'd choose between Flow and Apex, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: A full breakdown of this decision, including the save-order and maintainability reasoning, is in the deep dive below.
questions.professionalAnswer: I walk through the full reasoning -- and where I'd actually draw the line between Flow and Apex -- in the deep dive below.
commonMistakes: Choosing Apex or Flow as a blanket default without evaluating the specific requirement pieces separately
Missing that a calculation looping over an unrelated list is the part that genuinely pushes toward Apex
Not considering that the requirement could be split across both tools rather than forced into just one
Overlooking maintainability -- who can read and update this logic later
keyPoints: Break a multi-part requirement into its individual pieces before choosing a tool
Simple record updates and notifications are squarely within Flow's native capability
A loop over an unrelated collection for a calculation is a genuine signal to use Apex
The two tools can be combined -- Flow calling an Apex action for the one piece that needs it
Maintainability and who can read the logic later matters as much as raw capability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly decomposes the requirement into separately evaluable pieces
Correctly identifies which pieces fit Flow vs. which need Apex
Gives sound reasoning for a combined or hybrid approach

deepDive.heading: Break the requirement into its real pieces
deepDive.content: This isn't one decision, it's several, bundled into one request. Updating three related records across two objects when an Opportunity closes Won is well within declarative territory -- that's exactly what record-triggered Flow with related-record update actions is built for. Sending a notification is also a native Flow action. The piece that actually changes the calculus is the calculation involving a loop over an unrelated list of pricing tiers for a subset of deal types -- that's a different shape of problem entirely, and it's the one piece worth scrutinizing closely before picking a tool for the whole thing.

deepDive.heading: Why the simple pieces belong in Flow
deepDive.content: Updating related records and sending a notification are same-transaction, declarative-native operations. Building them in Apex instead would mean writing, testing, and maintaining code for logic that a non-developer admin could otherwise read and adjust directly in Flow Builder -- a real maintainability cost with no corresponding capability benefit, since Flow already does this natively and efficiently.

deepDive.heading: Why the pricing-tier calculation pushes toward Apex
deepDive.content: Looping over an unrelated collection (pricing tiers that aren't directly related records on the Opportunity) to perform a calculation is the kind of iterative, data-structure-manipulation logic Flow's loop element can technically do, but awkwardly and with weaker performance and readability at any real complexity. If the calculation involves conditional branching across tiers, intermediate variables, or logic that would benefit from unit tests (especially if pricing calculations feed into revenue recognition or reporting that compliance cares about), that's a concrete, defensible reason to write this piece in Apex.

deepDive.heading: The decision: a hybrid approach, not an either/or
deepDive.content: The right design here is a record-triggered Flow handling the simple related-record updates and the notification natively, which then calls an Apex-defined invocable action specifically for the pricing-tier calculation on the subset of deal types that need it. This keeps the bulk of the logic visible and admin-maintainable in Flow Builder, while isolating the one piece that genuinely needs code into a small, focused, unit-testable Apex class -- rather than either forcing the whole thing into an awkward all-Flow build, or writing a full Apex trigger that reimplements simple record updates Flow already handles well.

deepDive.heading: What a weaker answer misses
deepDive.content: A junior answer picks one tool for the entire requirement without decomposing it -- either 'it's complex, so Apex' (ignoring that most of the requirement is simple and better served by Flow) or 'declarative-first, so Flow' (ignoring that the pricing-tier loop is a genuine complexity signal). The stronger answer treats the decision as modular: evaluate each piece of a bundled requirement independently, and don't let the hardest part of the ask dictate the tool for the easiest parts.

questions.title: Choosing LWC vs. Visualforce for a New Internal Tool
questions.prompt: A team wants a new custom internal screen built on the Salesforce platform: an interactive data-entry page with dynamic client-side validation and a modern look. Would you build it in Lightning Web Components or Visualforce, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: LWC is the correct choice here. Visualforce was designed in an era before Lightning Experience and relies more heavily on server round-trips for interactivity, with a dated look unless heavily customized, while LWC is built on modern web standards, renders natively inside Lightning Experience, and supports rich, responsive client-side interactivity (dynamic validation, reactive UI updates) without full-page server reloads. The only scenario that would push toward Visualforce instead is a narrow technical need Visualforce still uniquely covers, like rendering a page as a PDF -- which doesn't apply to an interactive data-entry screen.
questions.professionalAnswer: For something like this, I wouldn't even seriously weigh Visualforce -- LWC is what this is built for. Visualforce's whole model leans on server round-trips for a lot of its interactivity, which feels clunky for something that's supposed to have dynamic, responsive validation as the user types. LWC gives me real client-side reactivity, a current look that matches the rest of Lightning Experience without extra styling effort, and it's what Salesforce is investing in going forward. The only time I'd reach for Visualforce today is something narrow like generating a PDF, which isn't what's being asked for here at all.
commonMistakes: Choosing Visualforce out of familiarity rather than evaluating actual fit for an interactive UI
Not recognizing LWC's native, modern-standards-based reactivity is the better fit for dynamic validation
Overlooking that Visualforce still has a narrow, legitimate niche (like PDF rendering)
Assuming the choice doesn't matter because 'they're both Salesforce UI tools'
keyPoints: LWC is built on modern web standards and supports rich client-side interactivity natively
Visualforce relies more on server round-trips, which fits less well for dynamic, reactive UI
LWC matches the current Lightning Experience look without extra styling effort
Visualforce retains a narrow legitimate use (like PDF rendering), but not for this scenario

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends LWC with sound technical reasoning
Correctly characterizes Visualforce's remaining narrow use cases
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: REST API vs. Bulk API for an Integration Scenario
questions.prompt: An external e-commerce system needs to sync order data into Salesforce. Most days it's a handful of new orders trickling in throughout the day, but once a quarter it needs to backfill around 500,000 historical order records in one go. Would you use the REST API, the Bulk API, or both, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Both APIs are appropriate here, for different parts of the workload. The REST API is well suited to the day-to-day trickle of individual new orders -- low-latency, synchronous, record-at-a-time (or small-batch) operations are exactly what it's designed for, and using it for a handful of records per day is efficient and simple. The Bulk API is purpose-built for the quarterly 500,000-record backfill -- it's designed for large-scale asynchronous batch processing, breaking the load into manageable chunks processed server-side, which would be far less efficient and far more likely to hit governor or API call limits if attempted through the REST API's per-record call pattern.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't force this into one API for both jobs -- they're genuinely different workloads. For the daily trickle of individual orders, REST API is the right tool: it's low-latency, synchronous, and perfectly efficient for a handful of records at a time. For the once-a-quarter 500,000-record backfill, I'd switch to Bulk API entirely -- trying to push half a million records through individual REST calls would be slow, would burn through API call limits fast, and just isn't what REST is built for. Bulk API is designed exactly for that kind of large, asynchronous batch load, chunking the work server-side instead of making the integration do that chunking itself.
commonMistakes: Forcing one API to handle both workloads instead of matching the tool to each use case
Using REST API for the large quarterly backfill, risking API call limits and poor performance
Using Bulk API for the daily trickle, adding unnecessary asynchronous complexity for a tiny, latency-sensitive workload
Not recognizing Bulk API is specifically designed for large-scale asynchronous batch processing
keyPoints: REST API fits low-latency, synchronous, small-volume operations well
Bulk API is purpose-built for large-scale, asynchronous batch loads
The two APIs can coexist in one integration, each handling the workload it fits
Forcing a large batch through REST API risks hitting API call limits and poor performance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches REST API to the daily trickle workload
Correctly matches Bulk API to the quarterly backfill workload
Explains why forcing one API for both would be the wrong design

questions.title: Designing a Basic Data Model for a New Business Relationship
questions.prompt: A client wants to track Vendors and the Products each Vendor supplies, where the same Product can be supplied by multiple Vendors at different prices. Sketch out the basic object model you'd propose.
questions.modelAnswer: Vendor and Product is a many-to-many relationship -- a Vendor supplies many Products, and a Product can come from many Vendors -- so it needs a junction object between them, commonly named something like Vendor Product (or Supply Agreement), with a relationship field to Vendor and a relationship field to Product. Critically, since price varies per Vendor-Product pairing rather than being a fixed attribute of either side alone, the price field belongs on the junction object itself, not on Vendor or Product directly -- each junction record represents one specific Vendor's price for one specific Product.
questions.professionalAnswer: The giveaway that this needs a junction object is 'the same Product can be supplied by multiple Vendors' -- that's a many-to-many relationship, which Salesforce's relationship fields can't represent directly. So I'd create a Vendor Product object sitting between Vendor and Product, with a relationship field to each. The detail I'd make sure not to miss is where the price lives: since price depends on the specific Vendor-Product combination, not on the Vendor or the Product alone, it has to be a field on the junction object itself. If I put it on Product instead, I'd have no way to represent that Vendor A charges $10 and Vendor B charges $12 for the exact same Product.
commonMistakes: Trying to model the relationship with a direct lookup on Vendor or Product instead of a junction object
Putting the price field on Vendor or Product instead of on the junction object
Not recognizing 'supplied by multiple Vendors at different prices' as the signal for a many-to-many relationship
Choosing master-detail without considering whether the junction record should survive independently of either parent
keyPoints: Vendor-to-Product is a many-to-many relationship, requiring a junction object
The junction object needs a relationship field to both Vendor and Product
Price, since it varies per Vendor-Product pairing, belongs on the junction object
Each junction record represents one specific Vendor's terms for one specific Product

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the need for a junction object
Correctly places the price field on the junction object
Clarity of the proposed model

questions.title: CRM Analytics vs. Standard Reports for a New Reporting Need
questions.prompt: A sales operations team wants to analyze Opportunity trends alongside marketing spend data that lives in an external spreadsheet-based system, slicing by several dimensions interactively. Would you build this with standard Salesforce reports and dashboards, or CRM Analytics, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: CRM Analytics is the better fit here. The requirement explicitly needs to blend Salesforce Opportunity data with marketing spend data from an external, non-Salesforce source -- something standard reports and dashboards fundamentally can't do, since they only report against live Salesforce records. CRM Analytics is designed exactly for this: it can ingest and blend data from multiple sources into one dataset, and its lens-based exploration supports the kind of interactive, multi-dimensional slicing the sales ops team is asking for, well beyond what a standard report's filters and groupings offer.
questions.professionalAnswer: The deciding factor for me is the marketing spend data living outside Salesforce entirely -- standard reports and dashboards simply can't blend in an external data source, full stop, so that alone rules them out for this exact requirement. CRM Analytics is built precisely for this situation: I can bring in that external spend data alongside the Salesforce Opportunity data into one blended dataset, and then let the team explore it interactively with a lens, slicing across whatever dimensions they want, which goes well beyond what report filters and groupings can offer. If the ask were purely Salesforce Opportunity data with simple filtering, I'd push back toward a standard report instead, since CRM Analytics is real overhead that isn't worth it for something simpler -- but blending external data is exactly the line that justifies it here.
commonMistakes: Trying to force standard reports/dashboards to handle data that lives outside Salesforce
Choosing CRM Analytics by default without first checking whether a simpler standard report would suffice
Not identifying the external data blending requirement as the deciding factor
Underselling CRM Analytics's interactive, multi-dimensional lens exploration as 'just another dashboard'
keyPoints: Standard reports and dashboards can only report against live Salesforce data, not external sources
CRM Analytics can blend Salesforce data with external data sources into one dataset
The explicit need to combine external marketing spend data is the deciding factor here
CRM Analytics's lens-based exploration supports richer, interactive multi-dimensional slicing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends CRM Analytics with sound reasoning
Correctly identifies the external-data-blending need as the deciding factor
Notes when a standard report would have been the simpler, sufficient choice

questions.title: Explaining Why a Change Needs Apex to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: A product manager is frustrated that a request they thought was 'simple' -- a calculation on Opportunity -- is going to take a developer and two days instead of an afternoon in Flow. How do you explain the technical tradeoff to them in a way that doesn't feel like a brush-off?
questions.modelAnswer: A good answer avoids jargon-heavy justification and instead translates the technical constraint into terms the stakeholder already cares about: cost, risk, and timeline. It explains concretely what makes this specific calculation different from a 'simple' one -- for example, that it needs to loop over data Flow can't efficiently handle, or that it needs to be unit-tested because it affects revenue reporting -- using a plain analogy rather than platform jargon, and offers a path forward (what can ship quickly now versus what needs the extra two days) instead of just delivering a timeline and ending the conversation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't start with 'well, Flow can't do bulkified loops over heap-constrained collections' -- that's going to land as a wall of jargon, not an explanation. I'd say something like, 'most of what we build in Flow is quick because it's made for simple, direct changes -- think of it like filling out a form. This particular calculation needs real looping logic over a separate set of data, which is more like writing a small program than filling out a form, and that needs a developer and some testing to make sure it's right, especially since it touches revenue numbers.' Then I'd try to give them something concrete they can act on -- like offering to ship a simpler version now and the full calculation in two days, so they're not just hearing 'no' and a delay.
commonMistakes: Explaining the technical constraint using jargon the stakeholder doesn't understand
Framing the explanation as a flat 'it's just more complicated' without a concrete reason why
Not offering any interim option or path forward, leaving the stakeholder with just a delay
Sounding defensive or dismissive instead of collaborative
keyPoints: Translate the technical constraint into terms like cost, risk, and timeline rather than jargon
Use a concrete, plain-language analogy for what makes this requirement different
Tie the complexity to something the stakeholder cares about, like reporting accuracy
Offer a path forward or interim option rather than ending on just a delay

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the tradeoff in plain, non-jargon terms
Gives a concrete, accurate reason for the complexity
Offers a constructive path forward rather than just a delay

questions.title: Asking for Help When Stuck on a Governor-Limit Bug
questions.prompt: You've spent half a day stuck on an Apex governor-limit error you can't figure out, and a senior developer on the team is clearly busy. How do you approach asking for help in a way that respects their time and still gets you unstuck?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids both extremes -- silently struggling for hours out of pride, and interrupting with an under-prepared 'it's broken, help' ask. It describes doing the groundwork first: isolating the specific error message, identifying exactly which line or method triggers it, trying at least one or two targeted fixes based on understanding what the error actually means, and writing all of that down concisely. The ask itself should be specific and time-bounded -- for example, a short written summary with the error, what's been tried, and a direct question, sent asynchronously first so the senior developer can respond when they have a moment, rather than demanding an immediate interruption.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just sit on it for another three hours out of pride, but I also wouldn't walk over and say 'it's broken, can you help' without having done any legwork first. I'd spend the time narrowing it down myself -- what's the exact error, which line is actually throwing it, and what have I already tried based on what I think the error means -- and write that up concisely. Then, since I know they're busy, I'd send it async, something like: 'Hitting a too-many-SOQL-queries error in this method, here's what I've tried, here's my best guess at the cause, do you have 10 minutes today or should I keep digging?' That respects their time because they can glance at it and reply when they actually have a moment, and it shows I didn't just give up at the first sign of trouble.
commonMistakes: Struggling in isolation for far too long instead of asking for help at a reasonable point
Asking for help with no specifics -- just 'it's broken' with no error message or context
Demanding an immediate interruption instead of a time-respecting, asynchronous ask
Not showing what's already been tried, making the senior developer start from zero
keyPoints: Do real diagnostic legwork before asking, and document it concisely
Include the specific error, what's been tried, and a direct question
Prefer an asynchronous, time-bounded ask over demanding an immediate interruption
Asking for help at a reasonable point is a sign of good judgment, not a weakness

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes doing real diagnostic groundwork before asking
Crafts a specific, well-documented ask
Respects the senior developer's time appropriately

questions.title: Documenting an Architecture Decision for Future Reference
questions.prompt: You chose to build a particular piece of logic in Apex instead of Flow, for specific technical reasons. Six months from now, someone else will inherit this and might wonder why. What would you actually write down, and where?
questions.modelAnswer: A good answer describes writing a short, lightweight decision record -- not a long formal document -- capturing what was decided, the specific technical reason that forced the decision (not a vague 'it was simpler'), what alternatives were considered and why they were rejected, and the date. This belongs somewhere a future maintainer will actually find it: a comment at the top of the Apex class itself, and/or a brief entry in the team's shared architecture documentation or decision log, rather than only in a chat message or a ticket that will eventually be archived and hard to search.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it short on purpose, because a long document nobody reads is worse than no document. At the top of the Apex class itself, I'd put a short comment: what this does, and specifically why it's Apex instead of Flow -- something concrete like 'needs a loop over an unrelated pricing-tier list that Flow can't handle cleanly, see ticket #1234.' Then I'd also drop a short entry in our team's decision log if we keep one, because six months from now, whoever inherits this shouldn't have to reverse-engineer my reasoning from the code alone, and they definitely shouldn't have to dig through old chat messages to find out why. The goal is that someone finds the 'why' in the same place they find the code, not in a separate place they'd have to know to look for.
commonMistakes: Writing no documentation at all and relying on memory or chat history
Writing something vague like 'this was simpler' instead of the specific technical reason
Putting the explanation only in a ticket or chat message that will be hard to find later
Over-documenting with a long formal document nobody will actually read
keyPoints: Document the specific technical reason, not a vague justification
Note what alternatives were considered and why they were rejected
Put the explanation where a future maintainer will actually find it, like a code comment
Keep it short and lightweight rather than a long document nobody reads

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes capturing a specific, concrete technical reason
Chooses a sensible, discoverable location for the documentation
Keeps the documentation appropriately lightweight

questions.title: Responding to Code Review Feedback Professionally
questions.prompt: You submit your first real Apex pull request on a new team, and a reviewer leaves several comments pointing out missing bulkification and a lack of test coverage. How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer treats the feedback as normal, expected, and useful rather than as criticism to be defensive about -- especially for someone newer to enterprise Apex practices. It describes actually understanding each piece of feedback (asking a clarifying question if a comment isn't fully clear, rather than guessing), making the requested changes, and, where it adds value, briefly explaining back what was learned, so the reviewer can confirm the understanding is correct rather than just seeing the diff change. It avoids defensiveness, over-apologizing, or silently making changes without engaging with the 'why' behind the feedback.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, on a first PR on a new team, I'd expect feedback like this and not take it personally at all -- bulkification and test coverage are exactly the kind of things a reviewer should be catching, and getting that feedback early is better than it slipping through. I'd read through each comment, and if one wasn't fully clear to me, I'd just ask -- something like 'just to confirm, you want this query moved outside the loop here, right?' -- rather than guessing and resubmitting something that still misses the point. Once I make the changes, I'd probably add a short note back like 'moved the query outside the loop and added test coverage for the bulk case, thanks for catching that' -- partly so they know it's addressed, and partly so they can tell I actually understood why, not just that I changed some lines.
commonMistakes: Responding defensively or taking the feedback personally
Silently making changes without confirming understanding of unclear feedback
Over-apologizing instead of simply addressing the feedback professionally
Not following up to confirm the changes actually address what the reviewer flagged
keyPoints: Treat code review feedback as normal and useful, not as personal criticism
Ask clarifying questions rather than guessing at unclear feedback
Make the requested changes and briefly confirm understanding back to the reviewer
Avoid both defensiveness and excessive apologizing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows a non-defensive, growth-oriented attitude toward feedback
Describes clarifying unclear feedback rather than guessing
Describes closing the loop with the reviewer after making changes

questions.title: Asking Clarifying Questions Before Starting a Design Task
questions.prompt: A senior architect hands you a one-paragraph description of a new integration and asks you to sketch a first draft of the approach. The description leaves out several important details. What do you do before you start designing?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer resists the urge to start designing immediately on an incomplete picture, and instead identifies the specific gaps that would materially change the design -- for example, expected data volume, whether the integration needs to be real-time or can be batch, which system initiates the connection, and what should happen on failure. It describes asking those as a short, specific list of questions rather than one vague 'can you give me more details,' so the senior architect can answer efficiently, and explains that getting these specifics right up front avoids designing something that has to be thrown away once the real constraints surface later.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just start sketching boxes and arrows off a one-paragraph description -- that's how you end up designing the wrong thing confidently. I'd go back with a short, specific list, not a vague 'tell me more': roughly how much data are we talking about, does this need to be near-real-time or is batch fine, which system is actually initiating the call, and what's supposed to happen if the call fails. I'd keep that list tight and specific on purpose, because a specific list is easy and fast for a senior architect to answer in a couple of sentences, where a vague 'I need more context' just bounces the problem back to them without giving them anything concrete to respond to.
commonMistakes: Starting the design immediately on an incomplete picture to seem fast or capable
Asking one vague 'can you give me more context' question instead of specific ones
Not identifying which missing details would actually change the design materially
Guessing at critical details like data volume or real-time vs. batch instead of confirming them
keyPoints: Resist starting the design on a visibly incomplete picture
Identify the specific missing details that would materially change the approach
Ask a short, specific list of questions rather than one vague request for more context
Confirming key constraints up front avoids throwaway design work later

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Resists designing prematurely on incomplete information
Identifies specific, materially relevant missing details
Frames the questions concisely and usefully for the senior architect

questions.title: Pushing Back on an Unrealistic Estimate for Unfamiliar Work
questions.prompt: Your manager asks you to estimate how long it'll take to build an integration using Platform Events, a feature you've only read about but never actually implemented. They want a number today. How do you handle it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer avoids both extremes -- guessing a confident-sounding number to seem capable, and refusing to give any estimate at all. It describes being honest about the unfamiliarity upfront, giving a rough range based on comparable work or a quick time-boxed spike to reduce uncertainty, and being explicit about what could change the estimate once more is learned. It frames this as responsible estimating rather than a lack of confidence, since giving a falsely precise number on unfamiliar technology creates a worse problem later when the real timeline doesn't match.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just throw out a confident number to avoid an awkward conversation, because that number will come back to bite both of us when it's wrong. I'd be upfront: 'I haven't built with Platform Events hands-on before, so I can give you a rough range today, but I'd rather spend half a day doing a small proof-of-concept first so my estimate is actually grounded in something real instead of a guess.' If they genuinely need a number right now, I'd give a wider range than I'd give for something familiar, and I'd say explicitly what could move that number -- like whether we need ordered delivery or just at-least-once, since that changes the design meaningfully. That's not me avoiding the ask, it's me giving them an honest number instead of a comfortable-sounding wrong one.
commonMistakes: Giving a falsely precise, confident number on unfamiliar technology to avoid looking unsure
Refusing to give any estimate at all instead of offering a reasonable range
Not proposing a quick way to reduce uncertainty, like a short time-boxed spike
Not naming what specific factors could change the estimate later
keyPoints: Be honest about unfamiliarity rather than faking confidence
Offer a rough range, ideally informed by a quick time-boxed spike
Name the specific factors that could change the estimate once more is known
Frame this as responsible estimating, not as a lack of competence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Honestly communicates the unfamiliarity rather than faking confidence
Offers a reasonable, grounded way to provide an estimate anyway
Names what could change the estimate once more is known
